open-question.question: Where do the suite's per-host values live: the CLI command and its flags, the plugin directory in the built tree, the installed root, and whatever tool names and record shapes the tests read? Today they are Antigravity-bound module constants and fixtures in the suite's Python files, while everything else about a host is declared under scripts/hosts/<host>/, where adding a host needs no host-specific Python.
open-question.recommendation: The values only the suite uses stay beside the per-host record-reading code that uses them, while the plugin directory and the rendered plugin root each definition already declares are read from its settings.toml and typed nowhere a second time; the build's schema and template discovery stay untouched and no test data enters its input, and the suite runs only under the pinned interpreter, which has `tomllib`.
open-question.alternative: The values a host definition already declares, at least plugin_dir and the definition's own name and built tree, are read by the suite from scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml with tomllib; the values only the suite needs (the CLI command and its flags, the installed root, the tool names and parameter keys) and the per-host record-parsing code stay in the suite's Python as one per-host entry. The build and the definitions' key set are unchanged. No value is written in two places and the build still needs no change, since the suite only reads settings.toml, while the suite-only values that have no meaning to the build stay out of the build's input. A new host still needs host-specific Python in the suite for its CLI and its records, and the suite becomes a second reader of settings.toml, coupled to a format the build owns and validates for its own purposes; reading TOML ties the suite to Python 3.11 or later, which the pinned interpreter gives but the 3.9 floor run does not.

Every per-host value stays in the suite's own Python, generalised from today's Antigravity-bound constants into one per-host entry each for Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex: the CLI command and its flags, the built-tree plugin directory, the installed root, the tool names and parameter keys, and per-host code that turns each host's event records into the steps the tests read. The suite reads nothing under scripts/hosts/, the build and the host definitions are left unchanged, and the plugin directory each definition already declares as plugin_dir is written a second time in the suite. Nothing outside the on-demand suite changes: build_hosts.py, its SETTINGS_SCHEMA (which refuses any unknown settings key), and the committed hosts/ trees are untouched, and record parsing, which has to be code for at least the event-correlating shapes, sits in the same files as the values it reads. Adding a host then needs host-specific Python in the suite, breaking the rule that a host is a definition directory under scripts/hosts/ and nothing more, and the duplicated plugin directory (empty for Claude Code and Antigravity, plugins/cairn for Codex) can drift from the definition with no check catching it.

The declarative per-host values (the CLI command and its flags, the installed root or the rule for finding it, the tool names and parameter keys the assertions read) move into each host's settings.toml as one new table, added to the build's SETTINGS_SCHEMA so every definition must carry it with the same key set, and read by the suite with plugin_dir beside them. How each host's event records are parsed stays per-host code in the suite, selected by the record format the table names. Everything declarative about a host lives in its one definition and the build's existing identical-key-set validation catches a definition that forgets a suite value, so a new host's values are written once beside the rest of its declaration. The build is changed to accept and validate keys it never uses for rendering, mixing on-demand test data into the build's input, and a host whose record format is new still needs suite Python, so the no-host-specific-Python rule holds only for hosts that reuse an existing parser; how much record handling is needed at all depends on which record assertions the tests keep, an axis the host tool-call record question owns.

As the settings-table option, one new table in each host's settings.toml, added to the build's schema and read by the suite, but the table also declares each host's record shapes as data: which events are tool calls, where the tool name, its arguments, and its outcome sit, and how a call is matched to its result, all read by one generic parser in the suite with no per-host code. Adding a host needs no Python at all, in the build or the suite, which carries the definition-only rule for hosts over to the suite exactly. The three formats differ in structure, not only in names (Antigravity's step_update carries a final state per step, while Claude Code's stream-json and Codex's JSONL pair a call and its result across separate events), so the declaration needs a small mapping language and a generic parser for it, a large mechanism for three tests on an on-demand suite, carried in the build's input; it is worth building only to the extent the tests keep record assertions, which the host tool-call record question decides.

The declarative per-host values sit in a separate file of their own under each scripts/hosts/<host>/ directory, outside settings.toml, which the build does not validate; template discovery is taught to skip it as it skips slots/, so it is never rendered into hosts/<host>/. The suite reads it with plugin_dir from settings.toml, and record parsing stays per-host code in the suite. A host's suite values live with the rest of its declaration while the build's schema and validation stay exactly as they are, so test data never enters the build's input. The build still needs one change, a discovery skip, or the file renders into the shipped tree and is published to the distribution repository; no check keeps the side files' key sets identical across hosts unless the suite makes one, and a host with a new record format still needs suite Python.

As the side-file option, a separate file under each scripts/hosts/<host>/ that template discovery skips and the build does not validate, but it also declares the host's record shapes as data for one generic parser in the suite, so the suite holds no per-host code. Adding a host is a definition directory and nothing else, with the build's schema untouched and the suite's whole per-host knowledge, records included, declared beside that host's other settings. It carries both the discovery-skip change to the build and the mapping language and generic parser the structurally different record formats need, with no build validation of either file's shape; the parser's size depends on which record assertions survive, which the host tool-call record question decides.

The per-host values, record shapes declared as data included, live in one data file per host inside the suite's own directory rather than under scripts/hosts/, read by one generic suite parser; plugin_dir is read from the host's settings.toml, and neither the build nor the definitions change. The suite holds no per-host Python and the build is left wholly untouched, with no schema change and no discovery skip, and nothing a test needs can leak into a rendered or published tree. A host's declaration is split across two directories, so adding a host means a definition under scripts/hosts/ and a data file in the suite, against the rule that a host is declared in one place, and it still needs the mapping language and generic parser for the differently structured record formats, sized by which record assertions the host tool-call record question keeps.
